inline.text: Purpose:
Techniques for when the analytical question outgrows two variables — encoding a third dimension, screening many continuous variables at once, and handling genuinely cyclical data.
When the analytical question involves more than two variables, do
not
jump automatically to 3D charts. A 3D object rendered on a 2D screen often introduces perspective and occlusion problems without improving comparison.

blocks.text: 12.2 Why Size and Transparency Are Weaker Encodings

inline.text: Humans generally judge position more accurately than area or opacity. Therefore, size and transparency are better treated as secondary encodings rather than replacements for precise axes when exact comparison matters.
Faceting creates separate panels for subsets of the data. It is especially useful when the third variable is categorical or can be meaningfully binned.
Example:
Compare countries with life expectancy 50–60, 60–70, and 70–80 years in separate panels, then compare the distributions of schooling and GNI across groups.
More/smaller panels can increase precision but also increase eye movement and cognitive load. There is therefore a trade-off between
precision and scanning cost
Use a pair plot when you have a relatively small set of variables (roughly up to ten) and want a rapid EDA view of:

items.text: distributions. Categorical variables may appear as count/bar displays; continuous variables commonly appear as histograms.
pairwise relationships. Continuous × continuous commonly appears as scatter plots; categorical × continuous can appear as box plots or grouped distributions.

inline.text: For variables such as city, beds, price, and area, a pair plot can quickly reveal:

items.text: Which cities have different price distributions.
Whether area and price are positively associated.
Whether beds and area are correlated.

inline.text: A correlation heatmap is essentially a compact representation of pairwise relationships among many
continuous
variables. Instead of drawing every scatter plot, correlation strength/direction is represented by color.
Use it as a
screening tool
to find strongly related variables among tens of metrics.
A heatmap of Pearson correlations primarily summarizes
linear association
. It cannot replace inspecting scatter plots because nonlinear relationships can have weak linear correlation.

If customers rate multiple product features from 1–10, a heatmap can reveal groups of features that customers tend to rate similarly—for example, several price-related attributes may form a highly correlated block.
Parallel coordinates are useful when you have many continuous variables and want to inspect profiles, patterns, or clusters.
Each observation becomes a line crossing one vertical axis per variable. Variables are placed along the X-axis, and each variable is scaled so observations can be compared across dimensions.

blocks.text: Real use case: country development profiles

inline.text: Add GNI, HDI, life expectancy, schooling, and additional development metrics. Splitting/coloring by continent can reveal profile differences:

items.text: Europe: generally high non-income development metrics with wider GNI variation.
Africa: generally lower GNI with wider variation in other indicators.
South America: comparatively consistent profiles across several indicators.

inline.text: You can add many variables—ten or twenty is feasible—without creating a pairwise matrix.
With too many observations, line crossings create a visual "spaghetti" effect. Grouping, filtering, transparency, ordering variables carefully, and highlighting selected observations can help.

blocks.text: 14. Polar Coordinates, Pie Charts, and Rose Plots
14.1 Pie Chart = Bar Chart in Polar Coordinates

inline.text: Conceptually, converting a bar chart from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates turns bar lengths into angles. The resulting pie chart is generally harder to compare precisely than a bar chart.
Default rule:
prefer a bar chart when the analytical goal is accurate comparison of category magnitudes.

blocks.text:
flowchart TD
P{Does the variable have natural circularity?} -->|No| Bar[Bar / dot — not a pie]
P -->|Yes: clock, compass, season| Polar[Polar / rose is defensible]

inline.text: Polar coordinates are defensible when the underlying variable has
natural circularity
A rose plot can be understood as a histogram mapped onto polar coordinates. This is useful when the beginning and end of a linear axis are actually adjacent in the phenomenon.

A nocturnal animal may be active around midnight. On a conventional histogram, activity just before and after midnight can appear split at opposite ends of the x-axis. A polar representation joins the cycle, making the overnight activity burst easier to recognize.

blocks.summary: س: ما الفرق بين Histogram وBar Chart؟

inline.text: Histogram لمتغير مستمر واحد مقسم إلى Bins رقمية متجاورة لعرض التوزيع. Bar Chart لمقارنة مقياس بين فئات منفصلة (لا ترتيب رقمي متجاور بين الأعمدة).

inline.text: لأن طول العمود هو وسيلة ترميز الحجم، وقطع خط الأساس يضخّم الفروق الصغيرة بصريًا ويعطي انطباعًا مضللًا عن حجم الفرق الحقيقي.
Median (الوسيط)، Q1 وQ3 (الربيعان الأول والثالث)، IQR = Q3-Q1، Whiskers (عادة حتى 1.5×IQR)، والنقاط بعدها تُعتبر Outliers محتملة.

blocks.summary: س: عندك Correlation قريبة من الصفر بين متغيرين، هل هذا يعني عدم وجود علاقة؟

inline.text: لا بالضرورة. Pearson Correlation يقيس العلاقة
الخطية

blocks.summary: س: امتى تفضّل Dot Plot على Bar Plot؟

inline.text: لما تحتاج Log Scale (لأن الأعمدة لازم تبدأ من صفر والـLog لا يمثل الصفر)، أو لما عندك أكثر من مقياس لنفس الفئة وتحب تعرضهم على نفس الإطار الرقمي.

blocks.summary: س: ليه Stacked Bar ممكن يضلل رغم إنه شائع؟

inline.text: لأن الأجزاء غير الملاصقة لخط الأساس (Baseline) أصعب في المقارنة الدقيقة بصريًا. كل ما ابتعد الجزء عن الصفر، كل ما زادت صعوبة تقدير طوله الحقيقي.

blocks.summary: س: إيه الفرق بين Sequential وDiverging Color Scale، ومتى تستخدم كل واحد؟

inline.text: Sequential لمتغير مرتب من منخفض لمرتفع بدون منتصف ذو معنى (مثل عدد السكان). Diverging لما يكون فيه نقطة منتصف دلالية حقيقية (زي صفر في نسبة نمو، أو محايد بين سلبي وإيجابي) — استخدام Diverging بدون منتصف حقيقي يخلق انطباع مضلل.

blocks.summary: س: عندك KPI لازم يتعرض للإدارة التنفيذية في نفس الشاشة، إزاي تقرر الـChart؟

inline.text: ابدأ بالسؤال التحليلي والقرار المطلوب، بعدين نوع المتغيرات، بعدين اختار أبسط ترميز (Position أولاً) يوضح الرسالة الأساسية في ثوانٍ، مع خط أساس صادق وأقل Chartjunk ممكن، ولون له معنى واضح (مش زخرفة).

blocks.summary: س: امتى تستخدم Faceting (Small Multiples) بدل ما تضيف متغير ثالث بالـColor على نفس الرسم؟

inline.text: لما المتغير الثالث فئوي وعدد فئاته معقول (مش كبير جدًا)، وتحتاج دقة أعلى في المقارنة داخل كل مجموعة. الـColor على نفس الرسم أسرع للمسح العام لكن أقل دقة، والـFaceting أدق لكنه بيكلف مساحة وحركة عين أكتر — فيه Trade-off بين الدقة وسرعة المسح البصري.

blocks.summary: س: إزاي تتعامل مع Outlier ظاهر في الرسم قبل ما تفسّره كـInsight؟

inline.text: تتأكد الأول إنه مش مشكلة جودة بيانات (تكرار، إدخال خاطئ، Mixed Scales)، لأن تفسير Pattern قبل التأكد من صحة البيانات اللي أنتجته خطأ منهجي شائع.

blocks.summary: س: ليه الرسوم ثلاثية الأبعاد (3D Bars) غالبًا فكرة سيئة؟

Purpose:
How to choose color palettes that match the semantics of the data — the single most misused encoding in dashboards.
Color is one of the most useful additional encodings, but only when the palette matches the data semantics.

items.text: common in digital displays; specifies how much red, green, and blue light contributes to a color.
common in printing because it corresponds to ink channels.
designed around perceptual properties and therefore particularly useful for data visualization.
the perceived color family around the color wheel.
color intensity/saturation, from near-gray to vivid color.

inline.text: The key idea is that a technically valid color representation is not automatically a perceptually good data encoding.
Use for
unordered categories
Example: product types, technologies, departments.
Different hues distinguish categories; there is no intended low-to-high ordering.
Use for an
ordered variable from low to high
Example: population, consumption, risk score, or life expectancy.
Usually vary luminance or chroma while maintaining a coherent hue relationship.

central midpoint
Example: negative ↔ neutral ↔ positive, or strongly disagree ↔ neutral ↔ strongly agree.
The midpoint should have semantic meaning, not merely be mathematically convenient.

inline.text: Viridis is a widely used sequential palette designed with perceptual accessibility and grayscale-printing considerations in mind. It is especially useful when continuous values must be encoded by color.

if color represents ordered magnitude, make the ordering visually obvious; if color represents categories, do not imply a false order.

inline.text: Purpose:
The core chart-type library — the six workhorse plots plus the scale and trend-line concepts that support them.
A histogram visualizes the distribution of
one continuous variable
by grouping numeric values into intervals called
bins
and counting observations in each bin.
Example question:
At what ages did monarchs ascend to the throne, and which age ranges were most common?

items.text: usually count; depending on the implementation it can also represent density or another normalized quantity.
Each bar corresponds to an interval.

blocks.text: Bin width is a critical design choice

inline.text: A bin width that is too small can produce a noisy, jagged histogram. A bin width that is too large can hide important structure.
Therefore:
There is rarely a universally perfect bin width. Inspect several sensible choices and choose one that reveals the relevant structure without inventing noise.
Count the prominent peaks.
Multiple modes can suggest heterogeneous subpopulations or a mixture of processes.
Skewness describes asymmetry.
A reliable memory aid: the
tail points in the direction of the skew

blocks.alt: How to read a histogram - modality and skew — Unimodal, bimodal, and right-skewed histograms of the same kind of continuous variable.
blocks.caption: Unimodal, bimodal, and right-skewed histograms of the same kind of continuous variable.

inline.text: Kurtosis is a more advanced description related to tail/extreme-value behavior and concentration relative to a reference distribution. The terminology used in the lesson is:

items.text: relatively heavier tails / more extreme observations and often a sharper central peak.
relatively lighter tails / fewer extreme observations and often a flatter, broader center.

inline.text: Important caution: kurtosis should not be reduced to "peak height." Its interpretation is fundamentally about tail behavior and moments; different distributions can have similar-looking peaks but different tail properties.

items.text: Treating categorical values as histogram bins.
Choosing bins only because they look visually attractive.
Overinterpreting tiny fluctuations caused by binning.
Comparing histograms with incompatible scales or bin definitions.

inline.text: Multiple histograms can become difficult to compare when many categories are involved. Overlapping histograms can become a visual mess; separate panels consume space and make cross-panel comparison harder.
A box plot compresses each group's distribution into a compact statistical summary.
Use a box plot when you have:
A continuous variable split by a categorical variable, and you want to compare distributions across groups.

items.text: line inside the box; 50% of observations are below and 50% above it.
from Q1 to Q3, containing the middle 50% of observations.
conventionally extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × IQR of the quartile boundaries (implementation details can vary).
commonly displayed as potential outliers/far observations under the chosen rule.

blocks.text: What a box plot lets you compare

items.text: Differences in distribution shape/location between groups.

inline.text: A box plot is compact, but it hides information. Two groups can have similar box plots while having very different multimodal distributions. For small samples, raw points or a combination of box plot + points can provide useful additional context.
Use a scatter plot for
two continuous variables
when the goal is to understand their relationship.
Example:
Does house price increase as floor area increases?
Typical mapping:

items.text: positive, negative, or no clear direction.
how tightly points follow a pattern.
observations far from the general pattern.
whether the vertical spread changes with X.

inline.text: Correlation is useful for quantifying the strength and direction of a
linear
association.

items.text: Positive correlation: larger X tends to accompany larger Y.
Negative correlation: larger X tends to accompany smaller Y.

inline.text: A key warning:
Correlation is not a complete description of arbitrary relationships.

The Datasaurus examples demonstrate that datasets can share similar correlation while having radically different shapes. A curved, circular, clustered, or otherwise nonlinear relationship may have weak/zero linear correlation despite a strong non-linear relationship.
A fitted straight line can help diagnose whether a linear model is a reasonable approximation.
A smooth/curved trend line can reveal systematic non-linearity when a straight line is inadequate.
When variables span several orders of magnitude, log scales can spread observations more evenly and make multiplicative relationships easier to inspect.
A relationship that is approximately linear on a log-transformed scale can indicate multiplicative/exponential behavior in the original scale, depending on which variable(s) are transformed.
A line plot is closely related to a scatter plot, but it adds a crucial semantic condition:
Consecutive observations must be conceptually connected.
Time is the most common example because dates have a natural order and neighboring observations describe the evolution of the same process.
Multiple series can be shown together to compare trajectories, such as sales for several regions over time.
If a quantity grows by approximately a constant
absolute amount
per time step, its original-scale trajectory can be approximately linear.
If it grows by approximately a constant
percentage/multiplicative factor
, the original-scale trajectory can be exponential.
A log transformation of the Y-axis can turn an exponential relationship into an approximately straight line, making exponential growth easier to diagnose.

blocks.text: Critical warning: time on X does not automatically imply a line plot

inline.text: Suppose every point represents a different song released on a different date and the score is a critic rating. The observations are not successive measurements of the same evolving quantity. Connecting songs with a line would imply continuity that does not exist.
Use a scatter plot when the observations are not conceptually connected—even if the X-axis is a date.
A bar plot compares a
metric across categories
. Common metrics include:

Bars encode magnitude through their length/height from a baseline. Therefore, a zero baseline is conceptually important for honest magnitude comparisons. Truncating a bar chart can exaggerate differences.
Horizontal bars are often preferable when category labels are long, because they remain readable without rotating text.
Sort categories by the metric when ranking is important. This makes highest, lowest, and ties much easier to detect.
Stacked bars are useful when categories form components of a total and the total has meaning. A classic case is percentages summing to 100%:
This allows comparison of both total composition and how composition changes across groups/time.
Use caution when comparing segments that do not share a common baseline: stacked segments away from the baseline are harder to compare precisely.

items.text: usually one summarized metric per category.
distribution of many observations within each category.

inline.text: For example:
Average salary by department → Bar plot.
Distribution of salaries within each department → Box plot.
This distinction is essential:
Histogram bins represent adjacent numeric intervals; bar categories are discrete groups.
A dot plot can serve essentially the same category-versus-metric role as a bar plot, but it represents the value with a
point positioned on a numeric axis
rather than a bar extending from zero.
Bar charts depend on a zero baseline. A logarithmic axis cannot represent zero because:
A dot plot does not require the value to be represented as a bar extending from zero, so a logarithmic numeric axis can be used.
This is particularly valuable for quantities spanning several orders of magnitude, such as astronomical masses or other multiplicative measurements.
Dot-based displays can place multiple metric values for the same category on the same numeric framework, which can be more space-efficient and flexible than multiple bars.

items.text: visual distance corresponds to additive differences.
equal visual distances correspond to equal multiplicative ratios.

inline.text: For example, on a base-10 log scale, equal steps represent ×10 changes.
Both use points, but their analytical structures differ:

items.text: category + numeric metric; compare category-level values.
numeric + numeric; inspect relationships between observations.

items.text: Values span multiple orders of magnitude.
Ratios are more meaningful than absolute differences.
Exponential growth needs to be visualized.

Useful when the relationship is systematically non-linear. The curve can reveal acceleration, saturation, thresholds, or other structure.

headings.text: Variables Whose Treatment Depends on the Question

inline.text: Purpose:
The starting point for every visualization decision — why plots matter, how to classify your variables, and the master framework used throughout this reference.
A dataset can be summarized numerically, modeled statistically, or visualized. These approaches are complementary rather than competing.

items.text: mean, median, standard deviation, quantiles, proportions, etc. They compress data into numbers.
regression and other models quantify relationships, effects, uncertainty, or prediction.

inline.text: The Datasaurus Dozen contains datasets with essentially matching summary statistics—including similar means, standard deviations, and correlations—while having radically different shapes. The practical lesson is fundamental:

Before publishing a visualization, ask:

items.text: What exact question does this chart answer?
Are the variable types appropriate for the chosen plot?
Is the axis scale appropriate and clearly labeled?
Is zero meaningful and handled correctly for bars?
Are categories ordered in a useful way?
Are bins sensible and tested for histograms?
Does a line imply a connection that really exists?
Could a log scale reveal multiplicative structure?
Are outliers real observations, data-quality issues, or both?
Does aggregation hide important distributional information?
Is the chart readable without unnecessary decoration?
Could a different plot communicate the same insight more accurately?

rows.text: What is the distribution of one numeric variable?
Shows distribution shape and frequency across numeric intervals.
How does a distribution differ by group?
Compact comparison of median, quartiles, spread, and unusual observations.
How does a connected quantity evolve?
Which category has the largest/smallest metric?
Direct magnitude comparison from a zero baseline.
Which category has a value on a very wide multiplicative scale?
Can use a log axis without requiring a zero bar baseline.

blocks.summary: Trap 1 — "X-axis is Date, therefore Line Chart"

inline.text: False. A line requires conceptually connected consecutive observations. If each date corresponds to an independent item, such as a different song, a scatter plot may be better.

blocks.summary: Trap 2 — "Bar chart and histogram are the same"

inline.text: False. Histograms show a continuous distribution using numeric intervals; bar charts compare discrete categories using a metric.
False. Correlation primarily describes linear association. Nonlinear structures can have weak correlation.
Not by default. The central line is the median. A mean may be added separately depending on the implementation.

blocks.summary: Trap 5 — "More bins always means more information"

inline.text: False. Excessively narrow bins can turn random variation into visual noise.

blocks.summary: Trap 6 — "Bar charts can freely use a log axis"

inline.text: Not when the bars must originate at zero. A dot plot is a common alternative when a logarithmic category-level metric axis is required.

inline.text: Core principle:
The best chart is not the one that contains the most information. It is the one that makes the information relevant to the question easiest to see without introducing misleading visual implications.

inline.text: Purpose:
How charts mislead — bad baselines, dual axes, chartjunk, and common analytical pitfalls — plus the final design principles that tie the whole reference together.

blocks.text: Pitfall 1: choosing the chart before defining the question

inline.text: Bad workflow:
"I have data, so which chart looks good?"
Better workflow:
"What decision/question am I trying to answer, what variables are involved, and what structure do they have?"

blocks.text: Pitfall 2: confusing categories and continuous values

inline.text: Country is categorical. Age in exact years is quantitative. Age bands are categorical.

blocks.text: Pitfall 3: assuming correlation means relationship of any kind

inline.text: Pearson-style correlation is primarily about linear association. Always inspect the scatter plot.

blocks.text: Pitfall 4: assuming time always means line plot

inline.text: Check whether adjacent observations are conceptually connected.
Avoid truncating a bar baseline when the bar length is intended to encode magnitude.
Too many categories can make bars, labels, and colors unreadable. Aggregate, filter, rank, or redesign when appropriate.
A plot should maximize signal and minimize unnecessary visual complexity. Labels, scales, ordering, and annotations should serve the analytical question.

blocks.text: Pitfall 8: hiding distributional information in a single mean

inline.text: A mean can conceal skewness, multimodality, outliers, and unequal spread. Consider a box plot, histogram, or raw-point display when distribution matters.

blocks.alt: A mean is not a distribution — Same average. One team is unimodal. The other is two populations glued together.
blocks.caption: Same average. One team is unimodal. The other is two populations glued together.

inline.text: For bar charts:
The visual length of a bar should faithfully represent the magnitude of the value.
A truncated baseline can exaggerate small differences. This is especially dangerous for political polls, market shares, financial comparisons, and executive dashboards.
22.5% versus 21% is a difference of only 1.5 percentage points. A distorted bar scale can make the difference look dramatically larger than it is.

blocks.alt: Bar-length principle — Same two percentages. Zero baseline vs chopped axis.
blocks.caption: Same two percentages. Zero baseline vs chopped axis.

inline.text: The same baseline principle applies to stacked bars. If a market-share chart starts at 75% rather than zero, a large difference can visually appear small or vice versa.
Dual axes are tempting when two metrics have incompatible units or scales, but they can be misleading because changing either scale can change the apparent visual relationship between the series.
Use
separate panels
with clearly labeled axes. This makes it explicit that the metrics are different while still allowing aligned comparison.

Life expectancy may range roughly 50–90 years while HDI ranges from 0–1. A dual-axis chart can make their apparent correlation look strong or weak depending on the chosen axis ranges. Separate panels reduce this ambiguity.

blocks.text: 18. Chartjunk, Cognitive Load, and Sensory Overload

inline.text: A good visualization has two practical measures:

items.text: How many useful insights can the reader extract?
How quickly can they extract them?

inline.text: In a meeting or dashboard, the viewer may spend only seconds on a chart. The design therefore needs to optimize for rapid comprehension.
Chartjunk
= visual elements that make interpretation harder without adding meaningful information.
Common examples:

Skeuomorphism adds real-world visual characteristics to digital objects, such as shadows, physical depth, or realistic imagery. In data visualization these effects can distract from the actual encoding.
A standard bar chart already uses two dimensions:
Adding a third visual dimension without adding a third data variable increases complexity but not information. Perspective also makes endpoints harder to judge accurately.
Patterns such as stripes and cross-hatching can be difficult to distinguish, especially with many categories. Prefer a restrained palette and direct labeling when possible.
Good minimalism means:
Remove unnecessary visual complexity while preserving everything required to understand the data.
Labels, axes, legends, annotations, and gridlines can be useful when they reduce ambiguity. The objective is not minimum ink; it is maximum information per unit of visual complexity.

items.text: Use position before weaker encodings when precision matters.
Bar length must be proportional to value; use a zero baseline for ordinary bar magnitude comparisons.
Do not add 3D merely for decoration.
Use color according to semantics: qualitative, sequential, or diverging.
Do not imply order where none exists.
Do not imply a midpoint where none has meaning.
Correlation heatmaps summarize linear association; inspect the underlying data for nonlinear structure.
Use facets when separating groups improves clarity.
Use polar coordinates mainly for genuinely cyclical phenomena.
Avoid dual axes when separate panels can communicate the same story more honestly.
Remove chartjunk, but do not remove necessary context.
Optimize for insight density and speed of interpretation.
A beautiful chart that hides the truth is a bad visualization.

inline.text: Ultimate principle:
A visualization is successful when the visual encoding makes the important structure in the data easier to see, compare, interpret, and trust.
